entities.name: Edmund Beaufort, 2nd Duke of Somerset
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Edmund Beaufort, 2nd Duke of Somerset, a formidable English magnate and military commander, emerged as a central, divisive figure in the turbulent mid-15th century. His life, spanning from an unknown birth to his death at the First Battle of St Albans on May 22, 1455, directly precipitated the Wars of the Roses, England's devastating civil conflict. As a leading Lancastrian, his intense rivalry with Richard, Duke of York, for control of King Henry VI's government and influence over the ailing monarch, polarized the English nobility and shattered the fragile peace of the realm. His actions and ambitions fundamentally reshaped the political landscape of late medieval England.

Beaufort's career was marked by significant military commands during the final stages of the Hundred Years' War. He served as Lieutenant of France and Governor of Normandy, notably defending Caen in 1450, though ultimately surrendering it to the French. His military failures in Normandy, particularly the loss of Rouen and the disastrous Battle of Formigny in 1450, further eroded English prestige and contributed to the final collapse of English power in France, culminating in the loss of all continental possessions except Calais. Domestically, his ascent to power under Henry VI, marked by rapid accumulation of titles and offices, including Constable of England, fueled the deep resentment of the powerful Richard, Duke of York, who felt sidelined and dishonoured.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Edmund Beaufort's actions and intense rivalry with Richard, Duke of York, directly precipitated the outbreak of the Wars of the Roses in 1455, a conflict that reshaped the English monarchy and aristocracy for three decades. His military leadership, though ultimately unsuccessful in France, played a critical role in the final collapse of English continental power.
